final_message:
All five versions build with their own `build.cmd` and pass all three samples (`s1`, `s2`, `s3`), with output matching the expected files byte for byte.

**Extra testing.** I compared each version's output against a separate Python reference program on 10 more inputs:
- random graphs, from small up to the benchmark size (300k nodes, 900k roads);
- graphs split into many small clusters;
- a long path of nodes;
- many tied distances;
- a single node with no roads;
- a 300k-node grid with random shortcut roads, which is what `s3` looks like.

All five match on every one. They also all give the correct answer on a 2.5M-node path where distances go above 2³¹ (about 2.1 billion).

**Algorithm.** The program reads the whole file and parses the numbers by hand. It stores the roads in a compact adjacency layout (CSR): a start offset per node, and each neighbour stored as a (node, length) pair next to the others. Roads from a node to itself are dropped, since they can never make a path shorter. For each source it runs Dijkstra's algorithm. It uses a radix heap as the priority queue, which works because the distances it removes never go down. Queue entries are packed into one 64-bit number, distance in the high bits and node in the low bits, and outdated entries are skipped when popped. While popping it counts the reachable nodes, adds up the distances and tracks the largest distance with its smallest node number. On the benchmark-sized grid the radix heap ran about twice as fast as a 4-ary heap in C++.

**Speed choices per language:**
- **C++:** reads the file with one `fread`, uses plain vectors for the queue buckets, and sets stdout to binary mode. Without that, Windows writes CRLF line endings and the output no longer matches the expected files exactly.
- **Java:** reads with `Files.readAllBytes`, uses primitive arrays for the graph and the buckets, and keeps the queue state in local variables inside one `solve` method so the JIT optimises it well. Output is built in one `StringBuilder` and written once.
- **C#:** uses `unsafe` pointer code for parsing and the inner loop, and a `[AggressiveOptimization]` search method with its queue state in local variables. That change cut the grid run from about 650 to 560 ms. In the `.csproj` I also turned off concurrent and server garbage collection and set `TieredPGO`.
- **Go:** reads with `os.ReadFile`, uses `int32` arrays for the graph, `append`-based buckets, and `strconv.Append*` for output. Turning the garbage collector off made no difference, so I left it on.
- **JavaScript:** uses typed arrays throughout. When no distance can exceed 2³¹ (the program checks this from the road lengths), distances are kept as 32-bit integers, which made the search about 1.5× faster. Otherwise it falls back to 64-bit floats, which are exact up to 2⁵³, and builds the total as a `BigInt`. I tested that fallback separately by forcing it on.

**Rough times on the 300k-node grid test.** These are noisy, because other programs were running on the machine:

| Version | Time |
|---|---|
| C++ | ~0.33 s |
| C# | ~0.56 s |
| Go | ~0.55 s |
| JavaScript | ~0.9 s |
| Java | ~0.9–1.0 s |

My test files and scripts are in `tests/`: the input generators, the Python reference and `check.sh`. The benchmark doesn't use them, so you can delete that folder.

request.prompt:
You are writing five versions of the same program, in C++, Java, C#, Go and JavaScript, for a comparison of
how fast and how memory-hungry each version is.

The task is described in SPEC.md in this folder. The folder samples/ holds example inputs (`*.in`), each with
the exact expected output (`*.out`).

Each language has its own folder with a starting file and a `build.cmd`. The benchmark builds every program with
these same build scripts and flags, whatever you change in them. Write these programs:

1. `cpp/main.cpp` (more `.cpp` and header files in `cpp/` are fine): C++20, built by `cpp\build.cmd` with
   Microsoft Visual C++ 19.40 (Visual Studio 2022) and `/O2 /GL /EHsc /std:c++20`. Standard library only, plus
   nlohmann/json 3.12 (`#include <nlohmann/json.hpp>`, already in `cpp/include/`). Run as
   `cpp\solution.exe INPUT_PATH`.
2. `java/src/Main.java` (more `.java` files in `java/src/` are fine): Java 23, built by `java\build.cmd` with
   `javac`. Java SE only, plus Jackson 2.22 (core, databind and annotations, already in `java/lib/`). Run as
   `java\run.cmd INPUT_PATH`, which runs `java -cp "out;lib\*" Main` with the default JVM settings.
3. `csharp/Program.cs` (more `.cs` files in `csharp/` are fine): C# 12 on .NET 8, built in Release by
   `csharp\build.cmd`. Base class library only. You may change properties in `csharp/solution.csproj`, but do not
   add package references. Run as `csharp\out\solution.exe INPUT_PATH`.
4. `go/main.go` (more `.go` files in `go/` are fine): Go 1.27, built by `go\build.cmd`. Standard library only.
   Run as `go\solution.exe INPUT_PATH`.
5. `js/main.js`: JavaScript on Node.js 22, with no build step. Built-in Node modules only; no npm packages. Run as
   `node js\main.js INPUT_PATH`.

Each program reads the input file whose path is its first argument (SPEC.md says if a task takes more
arguments) and writes the answer to standard output exactly as SPEC.md describes.

Your goals, in order:

1. Every version must print the correct output for any valid input as SPEC.md defines it, not only for the
   samples.
2. Make each version as fast as you can. Write each one the way a skilled developer in that language would
   write fast code, using that language's own strengths.

Use a single thread and a single process unless SPEC.md says otherwise. Do not precompute or embed answers,
start other programs, or read any file other than the input. Python 3.13 (`C:\Python313\python.exe`) is
available if you want it for testing, but not as part of any program.

The programs will be run on Windows 11 on a 16-core laptop, on larger inputs of the same kind; SPEC.md gives
the benchmark size. Build and test all five versions against every sample before you finish. Work only inside
this folder, and take at most about 60 minutes. Other programs run on this machine at the same time: never stop
a process you did not start yourself, so do not kill processes by name (for example `taskkill /IM java.exe` or
`Stop-Process -Name node`); stop only your own processes, by process ID.

When you are done, reply with a short summary: the algorithm, the main choices you made for speed in each
version, and which samples each version passes.
